Chapter 8. Multi-Sample Experiments

Source: vignettes/articles/08-Multi-Sample-Experiments.Rmd
08-Multi-Sample-Experiments.Rmd

Each sample (each 10x channel) has its own suspension and therefore its own soup. When cells from several samples are analysed together, Decant gives every sample its own soup profile.

8.1 Why samples need separate soups

The soup reflects the cells that lysed in that particular sample. Two donors, or a control and a treated sample, can have quite different soups. Using one pooled soup for all of them over-corrects some genes in one sample and under-corrects them in another.

At the same time, a sample with few empty droplets gives a noisy soup. Decant handles both problems with partial pooling: a sample with many empty droplets keeps its own soup, and a sample with few is pulled towards the average of all samples.

8.2 Running several samples 

library(Decant)
mm <- simulate_multimodal(seed = 1)
empties <- lapply(mm$empties, function(e) e$unspliced + e$spliced)
sapply(empties, ncol)
#> [1] 3000  300 3000  300 3000  300

res <- decant(mm$obs_total, empties,
              sample_of = mm$sample_of, clusters = mm$labels)
res
#> <decant> 600 genes x 1500 cells
#>   modules : hierarchical_ambient, cluster_rho, correction_bayes_cell
#>   rho     : median 0.196 (10%-90%: 0.108-0.305)
  • simulate_multimodal() simulates six samples. Half have 3,000 empty droplets, half only 300.
  • The simulation stores spliced and unspliced counts separately; the second line adds them to get total counts per empty droplet.
  • empties is a list with one matrix per sample. Passing a list is what switches on per-sample soups (hierarchical_ambient in modules).
  • sample_of gives the sample of each cell, as a number matching the position in the list, or as a name matching names(empties).

8.3 Per-sample results 

dim(res$ambient)
#> [1] 600   6
round(rbind(estimated = tapply(res$rho, mm$sample_of, median),
            true      = tapply(mm$rho_true, mm$sample_of, median)), 3)
#>               1     2     3     4     5     6
#> estimated 0.201 0.203 0.189 0.188 0.198 0.192
#> true      0.197 0.195 0.186 0.183 0.191 0.195
  • res$ambient now has one soup column per sample.
  • The table compares the median estimated and true contamination in each sample. The estimates are within about one percentage point of the truth, including the samples with only 300 empty droplets.

8.4 The pooled soups directly 

pooled <- pool_soup(empties)
names(pooled)
#> [1] "pooled"      "independent" "lambda"      "mass"
pooled$mass
#> [1] 75064  7432 74846  7554 75017  7575
round(pooled$lambda, 2)
#> [1] 0.65 0.15 0.64 0.15 0.65 0.16
  • pool_soup() is the function decant() uses internally.
  • independent holds each sample’s own soup and pooled the soups after partial pooling.
  • mass is the number of UMIs in each sample’s empty droplets.
  • lambda is the weight each sample’s own soup receives; the rest comes from the average of all samples. Samples with ten times fewer soup UMIs (2, 4 and 6) rely on their own soup for only 15% and borrow the rest.

8.5 With Seurat

RunDecant() does the same when given one raw matrix per sample and a sample column (Chapter 6.5).
